title: New York’s Construction Reporting Pay Act: What Contractors Need to Know Before December 8
summary: New York’s Construction Reporting Pay Act takes effect December 8, 2026. Learn what reporting pay and cancellation pay mean for construction payroll.
body_markdown:
In construction, schedules change by the hour. A delayed concrete pour, missing materials, or unexpected weather can send an entire crew home before the workday even begins.


Starting December 8, 2026, those scheduling changes could come with new payroll obligations for New York contractors.


Under New York’s Construction Reporting Pay Act, certain last-minute shift cancellations and instances where workers report to a jobsite without receiving work will trigger minimum compensation requirements.


For contractors managing dozens of employees across multiple jobsites, this isn’t just another labor law. It’s another reason why scheduling, field operations, and payroll can no longer operate independently.


Here’s what you need to know.


## What Is New York’s Construction Reporting Pay Act?


Signed by Governor Kathy Hochul on September 9, 2026, the Construction Reporting Pay Act adds Sections 196-e and 224-g to New York Labor Law, establishing minimum compensation requirements when construction employees report to work but aren’t provided work, or when scheduled shifts are canceled on short notice.


The law introduces three key requirements.


### Up to Four Hours of Reporting Pay


Under the general construction provision, employees who report to work at their employer’s request but aren’t provided work must generally receive compensation for at least four hours or their regularly scheduled shift, whichever is shorter.


This compensation is calculated using the employee’s promised hourly rate.


For example, if a crew arrives at a jobsite only to discover that materials haven’t been delivered and work cannot proceed, the contractor may still be responsible for compensating those employees.


### Two Hours of Cancellation Pay


When an employer cancels a scheduled shift with less than 12 hours’ notice, affected construction employees are generally entitled to two hours of compensation.


Think about how often this happens in construction. Weather forecasts change overnight, inspections get delayed, and project schedules shift with little warning.


For contractors managing multiple crews and jobsites, accurately documenting when shifts are canceled and when employees receive notice becomes increasingly important.


### Additional Requirements for Prevailing Wage Projects


On covered prevailing wage projects, the law establishes separate compensation requirements.


Employees who report to work but aren’t provided work must generally receive at least four hours of compensation at their applicable prevailing wage rate, including supplements, for their scheduled classification.


Similarly, shifts canceled with less than 12 hours’ notice generally trigger two hours of compensation at the applicable prevailing wage rate, including supplements.


Where existing prevailing wage schedules establish more generous reporting-pay requirements, those provisions continue to apply.


For contractors already managing multiple wage determinations, classifications, and supplemental benefit obligations, these requirements add another consideration to an already complicated payroll process.


## What About Union Contractors?


An important distinction is emerging for union contractors.


According to guidance communicated by the Subcontractors Trade Association (STA), a pending chapter amendment is expected to exempt employees covered by collective bargaining agreements already in effect on December 8, 2026.


The Governor’s Office has indicated that the amendment is expected to apply retroactively to the law’s effective date, leaving no gap between December 8 and the amendment’s protections.


However, the amendment remains subject to legislative approval and the Governor’s signature.


Contractors operating under collective bargaining agreements should continue following their existing contractual requirements while monitoring the amendment’s progress and consulting legal counsel regarding their obligations.


## Why This Matters for Construction Payroll


Construction payroll is already among the most complicated in any industry.


A single employee might work across multiple jobsites, wage classifications, union jurisdictions, and prevailing wage projects in the same pay period.


Now consider a subcontractor managing 75 workers across six active projects.


A weather delay forces the cancellation of three crews with less than 12 hours’ notice. Each worker has a different wage classification, and some are assigned to prevailing wage projects.


The payroll administrator now needs to determine which employees qualify for cancellation pay, identify their applicable wage rates and supplements, and ensure the payments are processed correctly.


If scheduling happens over text, time tracking lives in one system, and payroll runs through another, the opportunity for errors is enormous.


The challenge isn’t simply calculating another two or four hours of pay. It’s ensuring that scheduling decisions, wage classifications, and payroll records remain connected.


And when those processes are disconnected, even small mistakes can create significant financial exposure.


Under New York’s wage-and-hour laws, payroll violations can result in back wages, penalties, and other liabilities. On public projects, compliance failures can carry additional consequences.


For contractors already operating on tight margins, these are risks worth getting ahead of.


## How Contractors Can Prepare Before December 8


With the effective date approaching, contractors should take a closer look at how their scheduling and payroll processes work together.


### Review Scheduling and Cancellation Procedures


Who has the authority to cancel a shift? How are workers notified? Where is that communication documented?


Whether cancellations happen through phone calls, text messages, or scheduling software, contractors should establish clear procedures for communicating changes and maintaining records.


### Evaluate Payroll Configurations


Payroll teams should confirm that their systems and processes can accommodate reporting-pay and cancellation-pay requirements.


This is particularly important for contractors managing multiple wage rates, prevailing wage classifications, and supplemental benefits.


### Review Prevailing Wage and Union Requirements


Not every employee or project will necessarily be subject to the same requirements.


Contractors should review applicable prevailing wage schedules, collective bargaining agreements, and the pending union exemption to understand how the law may affect their workforce.


### Train Field and Back-Office Teams


Payroll compliance doesn’t begin when someone submits a timesheet.


Project managers, foremen, and dispatchers make scheduling decisions every day that can affect employee compensation.


Those teams need to understand when a scheduling change may trigger a payroll obligation and how to communicate that information to the back office.


### Maintain Accurate Records


Accurate documentation will be essential.


Contractors should maintain reliable records of scheduled shifts, cancellations, employee notifications, wage classifications, and corresponding payments.


The more connected those records are, the easier it becomes to identify discrepancies and demonstrate compliance.


## Why Connected Field Operations and Payroll Matter


Most payroll systems weren’t built for the realities of construction. They were built to process hours and issue paychecks.


But construction payroll starts long before someone submits a timesheet.


It starts when a foreman assigns a crew, when a project manager changes a schedule, or when a worker moves between jobsites with different wage requirements.


New York’s Construction Reporting Pay Act makes that connection even more important.
